title: Experimental approach uses AI to eliminate cold storage for mRNA vaccines
source_used: Reuters (original blocked here: HTTP 401); read through Devdiscourse's copy of the Reuters Health Rounds item
key_facts: Researchers used AI to tweak the formulation of the lipid nanoparticles that carry mRNA in vaccines, making the particles more heat-resistant.
Current mRNA vaccines, including Moderna's flu shot, must be stored at very low temperatures, typically -40 to -86 Celsius.
The vaccines could stay stable at room temperature for up to a year, or at nearly 100 Fahrenheit for two months, according to a report in Nature Biotechnology.
Mice vaccinated with the particles, even after long-term storage, showed immune responses equivalent to mice given vaccines carried by particles similar to Moderna's original formulation.
The researchers say vaccines that tolerate higher temperatures could reduce storage costs by up to 86%.
Study leader Jinbi Tian of MIT says the approach could also apply to therapeutics and drug-delivery platforms.
quote_evidence: Using artificial intelligence, researchers may have found a way to make vaccines based on mRNA technology, such as Moderna's and Pfizer's COVID shots, storable at room temperature.

Cold-chain requirements add considerable infrastructure costs throughout the product life cycle, including specialized packaging, ultra-cold storage, temperature-controlled transport and continuous monitoring.
Our approach broadens the application of not only mRNA vaccines, but also therapeutics or advanced drug-delivery platforms.
why_it_matters_hint: Vaccines that do not need ultra-cold storage could cost less to deliver and reach places without that equipment, but the results so far are from mice.
